title: The Runaway Boat
text:
Once upon a time there was a fisherman who lived close by the castle and caught fish for the king’s table. One day he caught nothing at all. He baited and fished and fished and baited, but there wasn’t so much as a fishbone on his hook. Late in the day, a head rose up out of the water.

“Give me what your wife carries under her belt,” said the head, “and you shall have all the fish you want.”

The fisherman said yes on the spot. He didn’t know, you see, that his wife was expecting a child. And fish he got. From that day on there was a fish on every hook, as many as he could wish for.

But when he came home that evening and told his wife how he had come by such a catch, she began to weep and wail.

“God help me,” she said. “It’s a child I’m carrying under my belt!”

Word soon reached the castle that the fisherman’s wife was beside herself, and when the king heard why, he promised to take the child himself and do what he could to save it. The weeks went by and the months went by, and when her time came, the wife gave birth to a boy. The king took him in and raised him as his own son until he was grown.

Then one day the boy begged to go out fishing with his father, the fisherman. He wanted it more than anything, he said. The king didn’t like the idea, but in the end he gave in. All day long things went well, right up until they came ashore in the evening. Then the boy found he had left his handkerchief in the boat, and he jumped back in to fetch it.

The moment his feet touched the boards, the boat began to move. It went off on its own, straight out from the shore, with white foam churning around it. His father ran to the water’s edge and reached out after him, but the boat was already beyond his grasp. The boy seized the oars and pulled against it with all his might. It did no good. On and on the boat went, all night long, under a cold sky, until at last, far, far away, a pale white shore came in sight.

The fisherman’s son waded ashore, and when he had walked a little way, he met an old man with a long white beard.

“What’s this place called?” asked the boy.

“Whiteland,” said the old man. “And where have you come from, and what do you want here?”

The boy told him about the fisherman and the king and the boat that had run away with him.

“Well, then,” said the old man. “Walk on along this shore and you’ll come to three king’s daughters. They’re buried in the ground, so that only their heads stick up. The first one—she’s the eldest—will call out and beg you ever so sweetly to come and help her, and the second will do the same. But don’t you go near either of them. Hurry past as if you never saw or heard them. The third one you must go to, and do whatever she asks. That will be your fortune.”

It happened just as the old man had said. The first princess called out to the boy and begged him so very sweetly to come to her. He set his jaw and walked on by. He hurried past the second just as fast. But to the third he went.

“If you do as I tell you,” she said, “you may have whichever of us three you like.”

Well, he’d be glad to.

“Three trolls buried us here,” she said. “We used to live in that castle you can see over there in the forest. Now you must go into the castle and let the trolls whip you, one night for each of us. If you can bear it, we’ll be free.”

“I’ll give it a try,” said the boy.
imagePrompt: At dusk on a dark, rippling sea, the Fisherman’s Son—brave, newly grown and dressed simply—steps back into the small fishing boat to fetch his forgotten handkerchief, and the boat suddenly surges away on its own, churning white foam; his fisherman father stands helpless on the shore reaching after him as the boy strains at the oars, pulled toward a distant, pale-white shoreline under a cold sky.

title: Nine Heads in the Dark Room
text:
“There are two lions in the gateway,” the princess went on, “but if you walk straight between them, they won’t touch you. Go on into a small, dark room and lie down there. Then the troll will come and beat you. On the wall hangs a jar of ointment. Rub yourself with it wherever he’s struck you, and you’ll be as good as new. Next to the jar hangs a sword. Take it and kill the troll.”

The boy did as she said. He walked right between the lions without looking left or right, and they never stirred. Then he went straight into the little dark room and lay down.

The first night a troll came with three heads and three bundles of birch rods, and it whipped him till it was pitiful to see. But he held out until the troll was done. Then he took the jar and rubbed himself, grabbed the sword and killed the troll. When he came out in the morning, the princesses stood out of the ground up to their waists.

The second night went the same way, except that this troll had six heads and six bundles of rods, and it whipped him even harder than the first. In the morning the princesses stood out of the ground right down to their ankles.

The third night a troll came with nine heads and nine bundles of rods. It beat and whipped the boy for so long that at last he fainted. But the nine-headed troll wasn’t finished with him yet. It picked him up and flung him against the wall, and down came the jar. It smashed on the floor, the ointment splashed all over him, and in that instant he was as good as new.

He didn’t waste a moment. He wrenched the rods out of the troll’s fist, snatched the sword from the wall and killed the troll before it knew what was happening.

When he came out of the castle that morning, all three princesses were standing on solid ground. He took the youngest for his queen, and they lived well and happily together for a long time.

But in the end he began to long for home and his parents. The queen was none too keen, but he longed so badly that at last he simply had to go. Then she said to him:

“There’s one thing you must promise me. Do what your father asks you, but not what your mother asks you.”

He promised. Then she gave him a ring. Whoever wore it could wish for two things, anything at all. He wished himself home, and there he was. His parents couldn’t get over how grand and fine he had become.

When he had been home a few days, his mother wanted him to go up to the castle and show the king what had become of him.

“No,” said his father. “He shouldn’t. We want to enjoy him while we’ve got him.”

It was no use. His mother begged and pleaded until he went.
imagePrompt: Inside a small, pitch-dark chamber in the forest castle, a nine-headed troll looms with a bundle of birch rods as the battered Fisherman’s Son collapses against the wall—then the hanging ointment jar crashes down and splashes over him, healing him in an instant; he springs up with fierce resolve, gripping the wall-hung sword mid-swing, ready to hew the many-headed troll apart.

title: The Queen Vanishes
text:
At the castle the young king outshone the old one, in his clothes and in everything else, and the old king didn’t much care for that.

“Well,” he said, “you can see what my queen looks like. But I can’t see yours, can I? I don’t believe she’s as lovely as all that.”

“If only she were standing here, you’d see!” said the young king. And there she stood.

She was not happy. The courtiers gaped. The old king glared.

“Why didn’t you listen to me,” she said, “and do what your father told you? Now I must go home at once, and you’ve used up both your wishes.”

She tied a ring into his hair with her name on it. Then she turned her face away, wished herself home, and faded away before their eyes.

The young king was so grief-stricken that he went about day in and day out, thinking of nothing but how he might find his way back to his queen.

“I’ll just have to see if someone, somewhere, can tell me where Whiteland is,” he thought at last, and he set off into the world.

After a while he came to a mountain, and at the foot of it he met an old man who was lord of all the animals in the forest. He had a horn, and when he blew it, they came.

“Do you know where Whiteland is?” asked the king.

“No, I don’t,” said the man. “But I’ll ask my animals.”

He blew his horn, and they came from every side—bears and wolves, elk and deer, foxes and lynxes and hares—until the ground teemed with them. But when he asked whether any of them knew where Whiteland lay, not one of them did.

So the man gave the king a pair of skis.

“Stand on these,” he said, “and they’ll take you to my brother, a hundred miles from here. He’s lord of all the birds of the air. Ask him! When you get there, just turn the skis round so the tips point this way, and they’ll go home by themselves.”

It went just as the man had said. When the king got there, he turned the skis, and off they went home.

“Do you know where Whiteland is?” he asked.

The brother blew his horn, and every bird in the sky came flocking until the air went dark with wings. But none of them knew. Long after the rest came an old eagle. She had been away for ten whole years and had seen more of the world than any bird alive. She didn’t know either.

“Well, well,” said the man. “Then you’d better borrow a pair of skis from me. They’ll take you to my brother, a hundred miles from here. He’s lord of all the fish in the sea. Ask him! But don’t forget to turn the skis.”

The king thanked him, and when he got there he turned the skis, and home they went, just like the others.

“Do you know where Whiteland is?” he asked.

The third brother blew his horn, and all the fish in the sea came swimming until the water boiled with them. But none of them knew a thing. At last there came an old, old pike. She was so slow and heavy that he had to blow and blow before she arrived. When the king asked her, she said:

“Oh, yes, I know it well. I’ve been cook there these ten years. I’m going back tomorrow, because tomorrow the queen who lost her king is marrying someone else.”
imagePrompt: In the palace hall, the Jealous King glares while courtiers look on; the Fisherman’s Son, now a young king in splendid clothes, has just wished his queen to appear—she stands beside him, the Youngest Princess of Whiteland, clever and anguished, tying a ring with her name into his hair as a final token, her face turned sorrowfully away as she begins to fade back to Whiteland.

title: North Wind at the Castle Steps
text:
“If that’s how things stand,” said the lord of the fish, “I’ll give you a piece of advice. Out on a bog near here stand three brothers who have been fighting for a hundred years over a hat, a cloak and a pair of boots. Whoever has all three can make himself invisible and wish himself as far as he likes. Tell them you’d like to try the things, and then you’ll judge between them.”

The king thanked him and went out to the bog. There stood the brothers, fighting. They had been at it for a hundred years, and they looked it.

“What’s all this you’ve been fighting about, forever and ever?” said the king. “Let me try the things, and I’ll judge between you.”

They were only too glad. But once he had the hat on his head, the cloak on his back and the boots on his feet, he said:

“Next time we meet, you shall hear my judgment.”

And with that he wished himself away.

As he flew through the air, he fell in with the North Wind.

“Where are you off to?” said the North Wind.

“To Whiteland,” said the king, and he told him all that had happened.

“Well,” said the North Wind, “you’ll be going a bit faster than me. I have to get into every nook and cranny and gust and blow. But when you get there, stand on the steps by the door, and I’ll come roaring along as if I meant to blow the whole castle down. When the prince who’s marrying your queen comes out to see what’s going on, take him by the scruff of the neck and throw him out. I’ll see about getting him out of the way after that.”

The king did as the North Wind said. He stood on the steps by the door in the hat and the cloak and the boots, and waited. Soon the North Wind came howling and rushing, whipping up the snow, and it took such a hold on the castle wall that the whole castle shook. Out came the prince to see what on earth was the matter. The king grabbed him by the scruff of the neck and hurled him into the storm, and the North Wind caught him and carried him off.

When he was rid of him, the king went into the castle. At first the queen didn’t know him, for he had grown so thin and pale from wandering so long and grieving so much. But when he showed her the ring, she was glad with all her heart. And then the real wedding was held, and people talked of it far and wide.
imagePrompt: On the stone steps of Whiteland’s castle, the Fisherman’s Son stands firm wearing the stolen hat, cloak, and boots, while the North Wind roars like a living force, whipping snow and shaking the walls; the false prince stumbles out in alarm, and in one decisive motion the young king seizes him by the nape of the neck and hurls him outward into the raging wind that snatches the pretender away.
